title: Judah the Prince Writes It Down
bigQuestion: Why did the rabbis gather the Oral Torah into the Mishnah, and what does the Mishnah look like?

story.title: A Coffin and a Question
story.kicker: A rabbi leaves a city under siege the only way the guards will let him: as a dead man.
paragraphs: The year is 70 CE. Roman soldiers surround Jerusalem. Inside the walls, people are hungry, and fighters will not let anyone leave. A teacher named Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai wants to get out. He believes the city will fall. He wants to save something before it does.

The Talmud, in tractate Gittin, tells how he did it. His students spread the word that their teacher had died. They laid him in a coffin. Two of them, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Joshua, carried it toward the gate. The guards wanted to check with a sword. The students said: do you want the Romans to say Jews stab their own teachers? The guards let the coffin pass.

Outside the walls, the rabbi climbed out. He asked to see the Roman general, Vespasian. The story says he greeted the general as a king. Vespasian was not yet emperor, so he was annoyed. Just then a messenger arrived from Rome with news: the old emperor was dead, and Vespasian was to take his place.

The general said the rabbi could ask for something. Rabbi Yochanan did not ask for the city. He asked for Yavneh and its scholars, a small town where teachers could keep studying. He asked for the family of Rabban Gamliel to be spared. He asked for a doctor for a sick rabbi. Vespasian said yes.

That is how the Talmud remembers it. Historians say the story grew in the telling, but Yavneh really did become the center of Jewish learning after the Temple burned. In this chapter you will see what the teachers at Yavneh feared, and how, about 130 years later, Rabbi Judah the Prince answered that fear with a book.
story.think: The rabbi could have asked the general for anything. Why do you think he asked for a school?

lessons.title: Rome Burns the Temple
lessons.mainIdea: In 70 CE the Roman army destroyed the Second Temple, and Jewish life had to find a new center.
reading: For about a hundred years, *Rome* had ruled the Land of Israel. Roman governors taxed the people and put down protests. In 66 CE a *revolt* broke out. Jewish fighters drove out the Roman soldiers. Rome sent a large army. The general Vespasian led it, and later his son Titus.

In the summer of 70 CE, after a long *siege*, Roman soldiers broke into Jerusalem. They set fire to the Temple. Jewish tradition remembers that day with a fast. It falls on the ninth of the month of Av. The historian Josephus was there with the Roman side. He wrote a long account of the fall of the city.

The Temple had been the center of Jewish worship. Sacrifices could only be offered there. Now it was gone. Rabbinic tradition tells that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai comforted a student who wept at the ruins. He said that acts of kindness could also bring people close to God. Prayer, study and kindness became the heart of Jewish life.

words.d: the empire that ruled the Land of Israel from 63 BCE and destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE
a fight by a people against the rulers over them
when an army surrounds a city so that nothing can go in or out

look.title: Two Ways to Be Close
look.text: A student stands at the burned Temple and cries. He says the place where sins were forgiven is gone. His teacher says: do not be sad; we have another way that is just as good, acts of kindness. Rabbinic tradition, in a book called Avot de-Rabbi Natan, tells this story about Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai.
look.prompt: What is the teacher trying to give his student in place of the Temple?

check.q: Which empire destroyed the Second Temple, and when?
check.why: The Roman army under Titus burned the Second Temple in the summer of 70 CE. Babylon destroyed the First Temple in 586 BCE.

check.q: How does Jewish tradition remember the day the Temple burned?
choices: with a fast on the ninth of Av
check.why: The fast of the ninth of Av marks the destruction of the Temple in Jewish tradition.

check.q: What did Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai tell his weeping student?
choices: The Temple will be rebuilt next year
Acts of kindness can also bring people close to God
check.why: In the story told in Avot de-Rabbi Natan, the teacher says acts of kindness can take the place of the Temple's offerings.

lessons.title: Yavneh, a Town of Scholars
lessons.mainIdea: At Yavneh, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and his students rebuilt Jewish teaching around study and prayer.
reading: *Yavneh* was a small town near the coast, south of today's Tel Aviv. After 70 CE it became a center of Jewish learning. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai taught there. His students, and their students, are the first rabbis whose names fill the Mishnah. The word *rabbi* means my teacher.

The teachers at Yavneh made rules for a world without a Temple. Tradition says Rabban Yochanan made a ruling about the shofar, a ram's horn. It could be blown on Rosh Hashanah at Yavneh, as it once was in the Temple. Later, Rabban Gamliel led the school. Tradition holds that he helped set the order of daily prayer.

Historians see Yavneh as the start of *rabbinic Judaism*, the form of Judaism built on the rabbis' teaching. The Talmud tells its story with legends and details. What historians can say for sure is smaller. Both views agree that after the Temple fell, study and prayer became central.

words.d: a town in the Land of Israel that became the center of Jewish teaching after 70 CE
a Jewish teacher of Torah; the word means my teacher
the form of Judaism built on the rabbis' teachings, the Mishnah and the Talmud

look.title: Yochanan's Request
look.text: The Talmud tells that when the general said Rabban Yochanan could ask for something, he asked for three things. Give me Yavneh and its sages. Spare the family line of Rabban Gamliel. And send doctors to heal Rabbi Zadok, who had fasted for many years.
look.cite: Gittin 56b, paraphrased from the Babylonian Talmud
look.prompt: Each request saves something. What does each one save?

check.q: What does the word rabbi mean?
check.why: Rabbi means my teacher. The teachers at Yavneh are the first rabbis named in the Mishnah.

check.q: Where was Yavneh?
choices: in the Land of Israel, near the coast
check.why: Yavneh was a small town near the coast of the Land of Israel, south of today's Tel Aviv.

check.q: What do historians mean by rabbinic Judaism?
choices: Judaism of the priests at the Temple
the form of Judaism built on the rabbis' teaching
a group that rejected the Oral Torah
check.why: Rabbinic Judaism is the form of Judaism built on the rabbis' teachings, beginning at Yavneh and set down in the Mishnah and Talmud.

lessons.title: The Fear of Forgetting
lessons.mainIdea: War and persecution made the rabbis fear the Oral Torah would be forgotten, and that fear pushed them to gather it.
reading: The Oral Torah lived in *memory*. Every teacher held a piece of it. If a teacher died before passing it on, that piece could be lost. In the years after 70 CE, many teachers died. War, hunger and Roman punishment took them. The rabbis began to worry.

In 132 CE a second revolt broke out, led by Simon *Bar Kokhba*. It lasted about three years and ended in defeat. Rabbinic tradition says Rome then forbade the teaching of Torah. It tells that Rabbi Akiva kept teaching and was put to death. Many of his students died too. The rabbis moved north to the Galilee, to towns like Usha.

The teachers who survived did something new. They began to gather the teachings into short, clear sayings that could be learned by heart. Each saying was called a *mishnah*, from a Hebrew word for repeating. Students repeated them until they knew them cold. These collections became the raw material for the book you meet next.

words.d: the power to hold and repeat what you have learned
the leader of a Jewish revolt against Rome from 132 to 135 CE
as a small word, one short teaching learned by repeating; as a book, the Mishnah, the whole collection

look.title: Losses and Moves
rows: Revolt defeated; rabbis move to the Galilee
Mishnah gathered by Rabbi Judah the Prince (about)
look.cite: dates as commonly given by historians; the Mishnah's date is approximate
look.prompt: About how many years passed between the Temple's fall and the Mishnah? What could be forgotten in that time?

check.q: Why did the rabbis fear the Oral Torah would be lost?
choices: Because it was written in Greek
Because it lived in memory and many teachers were dying
Because the Sadducees had hidden it
check.why: The Oral Torah was held in memory. When war and persecution killed teachers, their pieces of it could be lost.

check.q: When was the Bar Kokhba revolt?
check.why: Bar Kokhba led a revolt against Rome from 132 to 135 CE. The first revolt ended in 70 CE.

check.q: What does the word mishnah come from?
check.why: Mishnah comes from a Hebrew root meaning to repeat. Students learned each teaching by repeating it.

lessons.title: The Man Called Rabbi
lessons.mainIdea: Rabbi Judah the Prince, leader of the Jews in the Land of Israel around 200 CE, gathered the Oral Torah into the Mishnah.
reading: *Judah the Prince* was born, tradition says, around the time of the Bar Kokhba revolt. He came from the family of Hillel. He became the *Nasi*, the prince or leader of the Jewish community under Roman rule. He was wealthy, respected by Roman officials, and a great scholar. The Talmud calls him simply Rabbi, the teacher.

Rabbi Judah lived in the Galilee, first in Bet She'arim and later in Sepphoris. He gathered the teachings of the earlier rabbis, the tannaim. He sorted them by subject. He chose which sayings to keep and how to word them. He kept many disagreements, naming who said what. Historians date the finished Mishnah to about 200 CE.

Was the Mishnah written on a scroll or held in memory? Scholars debate this. Some say Rabbi Judah arranged it to be memorized. Others say it was written down early. Either way, from about 200 CE on, the Mishnah was a fixed text. Every rabbi after him studied the same six orders in the same words.

words.d: the rabbi who gathered the Mishnah, c. 200 CE; the Talmud calls him Rabbi
the prince, the leader of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel under Rome
the rabbis whose teachings are in the Mishnah, from about 10 to 220 CE

look.title: Rabbi's Own Saying
look.text: Pirkei Avot records a saying of Rabbi, that is, Judah the Prince. He asked: which is the right path for a person to choose? One that brings honor to the one who walks it and honor from other people. He also said: be as careful with a small mitzvah as with a big one, since you do not know the reward for each.
look.cite: Mishnah Avot 2:1, retold from Charles Taylor, Sayings of the Jewish Fathers, 1877
look.prompt: Why might a person be tempted to treat a small rule less carefully than a big one?

check.q: What title does the Talmud give Judah the Prince?
check.why: The Talmud calls Judah the Prince simply Rabbi, the teacher. Ezra is the one called the scribe.

check.q: What does Nasi mean?
choices: the prince or leader of the Jewish community
check.why: Nasi means prince. It was the title of the leader of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel under Rome.

check.q: About when was the Mishnah finished?
check.why: Historians date the Mishnah to about 200 CE, in the time of Rabbi Judah the Prince.

lessons.title: Six Orders on a Shelf
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah is arranged in six orders by subject, and each order holds several tractates.
reading: The Mishnah is sorted into six orders. In Hebrew each *order* is a seder, the same word used for the Passover meal. The orders are Seeds, Festivals, Women, Damages, Holy Things and Purities. Together they hold sixty-three tractates, or books, each on one subject.

Seeds is about farming and blessings. Festivals is about Shabbat and the holidays. Women is about marriage and family. *Damages* is about courts, money, harm and fairness. Holy Things is about the Temple and its offerings. Purities is about what is clean and unclean for Temple purposes. Pirkei Avot sits inside the order of Damages.

The orders show what the rabbis cared about. Two whole orders are about a Temple that no longer stood. The rabbis kept studying its rules anyway. Jewish tradition holds that studying the rules counts as a kind of keeping them. Historians see it as a way of keeping the Temple alive in memory.

words.d: one of the six big parts of the Mishnah; in Hebrew, seder
the order of the Mishnah about courts, money, harm and fairness; Pirkei Avot is inside it

look.title: Tractates in Each Order
look.cite: the standard count of the Mishnah's 63 tractates
look.prompt: Add the six numbers. Which order has the fewest tractates, and what is it about?

check.q: How many orders does the Mishnah have?
check.why: The Mishnah has six orders. Sixty-three is the number of tractates inside them.

check.q: Which order holds Pirkei Avot?
check.why: Pirkei Avot is a tractate in the order of Damages, next to the tractates about courts.

check.q: Which order is about Shabbat and the holidays?
check.why: The order of Festivals covers Shabbat, Passover, Sukkot and the other holidays.

lessons.title: Short, Clear and in Hebrew
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah is written in short Hebrew sentences that state rules and record who disagreed.
reading: Open the Mishnah and you find short sentences. Each one states a rule or a case. The language is *Hebrew*, a plain and clear Hebrew that scholars call Mishnaic Hebrew. There is very little story and very little explaining. The Mishnah says what the rule is. It rarely says why.

The Mishnah also records *disagreement*. A rule will be stated, and then: Rabbi Judah says otherwise. Or: the House of Shammai say this, and the House of Hillel say that. The first tractate, Berakhot, starts with a question about when to say the evening Shema. Three answers are given, from three teachers.

Why keep the losing side? Rabbinic tradition gives an answer in the Mishnah itself. It says a court might one day agree with the lost opinion, so it must be on the page. The Mishnah is short because it was made to be remembered. It keeps the arguments because, to the rabbis, the arguing was part of the Torah.

words.d: the language of the Torah and the Mishnah
when two teachers give different answers to the same question; the Mishnah records both
a prayer from the Torah beginning Hear, O Israel, said in the morning and evening

look.title: The Mishnah's First Lines
look.text: The Mishnah opens by asking from what time the evening Shema may be recited. It answers: from the hour when the priests go in to eat their offering, until the end of the first watch of the night. That is the view of Rabbi Eliezer. The sages say until midnight. Rabban Gamliel says until the dawn comes up.
look.cite: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1, paraphrased from the Hebrew Mishnah
look.prompt: Count the answers in this one mishnah. Why do you think the text gives all of them instead of just one?

check.q: In what language is the Mishnah written?
check.why: The Mishnah is in a plain, clear Hebrew. The Gemara, which came later, is mostly in Aramaic.

check.q: What is the first question in the Mishnah?
choices: When may the evening Shema be recited?
How tall may a sukkah be?
What counts as work on Shabbat?
Who received the Torah at Sinai?
check.why: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1 asks from what time the evening Shema may be said, and gives three answers.

check.q: Why does the Mishnah keep an opinion that did not win?
choices: Because a later court might agree with it
Because the losing side wrote the book
check.why: The Mishnah says a later court might side with the lost opinion, so it stays on the page. The arguing was part of the tradition.

lessons.title: A Book That Asks for More
lessons.mainIdea: Because the Mishnah states rules without reasons, later rabbis kept asking why, and their discussion became the Gemara.
reading: The Mishnah solved one problem and made another. The Oral Torah was now safe in a fixed text. But the text was short. It said what the rule was, not why. A student who read that the evening Shema is said when the priests go in to eat would ask: why the priests? What time is that?

So the rabbis after Rabbi Judah studied the Mishnah the way earlier rabbis had studied the Torah. They asked what each line meant. They compared one mishnah to another. They brought in old teachings that were left out of the Mishnah. Each one is called a *baraita*. This discussion, in the Land of Israel and in Babylon, went on for about three hundred years.

That discussion is the *Gemara*. The word means completion or learning in Aramaic. Mishnah plus Gemara equals *Talmud*. So the Mishnah is like a seed. The Gemara grew from it, and the Talmud is the whole tree. The next unit follows that growing.

words.d: the rabbis' discussion of the Mishnah, gathered c. 400 to 500 CE; with the Mishnah it makes the Talmud
the Mishnah together with the Gemara; the word means learning
a teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in it; plural, baraitot

look.title: From Seed to Tree
look.text: Picture a page. In the middle is a short paragraph in Hebrew: the Mishnah. Around it grows a much longer text in Aramaic: the Gemara, asking what the short paragraph means. Around that, in smaller print, grow later explanations. The short paragraph in the middle is about the size of your hand. The page is as big as a tray.
look.prompt: Why would a short, clear rule book lead to a much longer book of discussion?

check.q: What is the Gemara?
choices: the six orders of the Mishnah
the rabbis' discussion of the Mishnah
check.why: The Gemara is the discussion of the Mishnah by later rabbis. Together, Mishnah and Gemara make up the Talmud.

check.q: What is a baraita?
choices: a teaching from the Mishnah's time that was left out of the Mishnah
check.why: A baraita is an early teaching not included in the Mishnah. The Gemara often brings baraitot into its discussion.

check.q: Mishnah plus Gemara equals what?
check.why: The Talmud is the Mishnah together with the Gemara. Torah is the five books; Avot is one tractate.

lessons.title: What the Mishnah Protects
lessons.mainIdea: Many of the Mishnah's rules protect people who could be hurt: the worker, the poor, the stranger and the person on trial.
reading: The Mishnah is not only about Temple and festival. Much of it is about fairness between people. In the order of Damages, one tractate says that a *worker* must be paid on time. Another is about lost objects. If a lost thing has a sign on it, the finder must announce it. Then the owner can claim it.

The order of Seeds has a rule for farmers. Leave the corners of the field for the *poor* and the *stranger*. This comes from the Torah. The Mishnah works out how big a corner should be. It treats these gifts as the poor person's right, not just as kindness.

Tractate Sanhedrin, about courts, is careful with people on trial. When a life is at stake, it says, witnesses must be warned first. One person, it says, is like a whole world. Rabbinic tradition reads these rules as *mercy* built into law. In this course, mercy and argument are the two threads to follow.

words.d: a person paid to do a job; the Mishnah says a worker must be paid on time
a person from somewhere else who lives among you; the Torah and Mishnah give the stranger a share of the harvest
care for someone who is weak, in trouble or in your power
people who do not have enough; the Mishnah gives them a right to the corners of the field

look.title: One Life, One World
look.text: Mishnah Sanhedrin says that a person was created alone at the beginning to teach that whoever destroys one life is counted as if he destroyed a whole world, and whoever saves one life is counted as if he saved a whole world. Some old copies of the Mishnah read one life of Israel; others read simply one life.
look.cite: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, paraphrased from the Hebrew Mishnah
look.prompt: This is said to witnesses before a trial for a person's life. Why would a court want witnesses to hear it first?

check.q: What does the Mishnah say about paying a worker?
choices: Pay only at the end of the year
Pay only if the work is perfect
check.why: The Mishnah, following the Torah, says a worker must be paid on time. This protects the worker.

check.q: Who gets the corners of the field, according to the Torah and Mishnah?
check.why: The Torah says to leave the corners for the poor and the stranger. The Mishnah in Seeds works out the details.

check.q: Why does the Mishnah say a person was created alone?
choices: To show that each life is like a whole world
To show that people should live alone
To explain why there are six orders
To warn against building a sukkah
check.why: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 says one person was created first to teach that each life counts as a whole world.

lessons.title: Two Chapters, One Chain
lessons.mainIdea: From Sinai to the Mishnah, rabbinic tradition tells one long chain of passing on and writing down.
reading: Look back at the two chapters of this unit. In rabbinic tradition, the *chain* starts with Moses at Sinai. It runs through Joshua, the elders, the prophets, the Men of the Great Assembly and the pairs. It reaches Hillel and Shammai. Then it reaches the teachers of Yavneh and, at last, Rabbi Judah the Prince.

Along that chain, the Oral Torah was spoken and remembered. Ezra read the Written Torah aloud and had it explained. The Pharisees defended the traditions of the elders. The Temple fell, and the rabbis feared forgetting. So Rabbi Judah gathered the teachings into a short, clear book: the Mishnah, c. 200 CE.

Different readers tell this chain differently. Orthodox tradition holds that every link goes back to Sinai. Many Conservative and Reform readers see a growing tradition shaped by people in each age. Historians test each link against evidence. All of them agree that the Mishnah became the *foundation* for everything the Talmud built next.

words.d: the line of teachers, each passing the tradition to the next, that Pirkei Avot describes
the base that everything else is built on

look.title: Links in a Line
look.text: Moses. Joshua. The elders. The prophets. The Men of the Great Assembly. Five pairs, ending with Hillel and Shammai. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai. Rabban Gamliel. Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Judah the Prince. Some of these are people, some are groups, and some of the dates are guesses. That is how Pirkei Avot lays out the chain.
look.prompt: Pick one link and say what you learned about it in this unit. Which link would a historian want more evidence for?

check.q: Which of these comes last in the chain?
choices: the Men of the Great Assembly
check.why: Rabbi Judah the Prince, c. 200 CE, gathered the Mishnah. The other links come before him.

check.q: What did the rabbis fear after the Temple fell?
choices: that the Oral Torah would be forgotten
that the Mishnah was too long
check.why: With teachers dying in war and persecution, the rabbis feared the Oral Torah held in memory would be lost. The Mishnah was the answer.

check.q: How do historians treat the chain of teachers?
choices: They say every link is certain
They test each link against evidence
They say the chain was invented by Rome
They only study the Written Torah
check.why: Historians check each link against evidence and say when a date is uncertain. Jewish traditions read the chain in their own ways.

review.q: How did Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai leave Jerusalem, according to the Talmud?
choices: in a coffin carried by his students
review.why: Gittin 56a–b tells that his students carried him out in a coffin, telling the guards he had died.

review.q: What did he ask the Roman general for?
review.why: The story says he asked for Yavneh and its sages, for Rabban Gamliel's family, and for a doctor for Rabbi Zadok.

review.q: Who gathered the Oral Torah into the Mishnah?
review.why: Rabbi Judah the Prince, called Rabbi, gathered the Mishnah in about 200 CE.

review.q: Which list gives the six orders of the Mishnah?
choices: Seeds, Festivals, Women, Damages, Holy Things, Purities
Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua
Berakhot, Shabbat, Sukkah, Pesachim, Avot, Sanhedrin
Moses, Joshua, elders, prophets, pairs, rabbis
review.why: The six orders are Seeds, Festivals, Women, Damages, Holy Things and Purities. The second list is Bible books; the third is tractates.

review.q: How many tractates does the Mishnah have?
review.why: The Mishnah has sixty-three tractates in six orders. Thirty-nine is the number of kinds of Shabbat work.
The Mishnah is written in short, clear Hebrew sentences that state rules and record who disagreed.

review.q: What grew out of the Mishnah to make the Talmud?
review.why: The Gemara is the rabbis' discussion of the Mishnah. Mishnah plus Gemara equals Talmud.

review.q: Which rule shows mercy built into the Mishnah's law?
choices: A worker must be paid on time
A sukkah may not be over twenty cubits tall
The evening Shema is said until midnight
Priests eat their offering at nightfall
review.why: Paying a worker on time protects the worker. The other rules are about festival and prayer times, not mercy.
